title: TESA — Telerobotic Endovascular Skills Assessment
tagline: Endovascular robotics · Open data and hardware
summary: A low-cost open-source guidewire robot and standardized dataset for endovascular navigation, contributed to the Open-H Endoluminal initiative.
body: Endovascular procedures such as mechanical thrombectomy depend on navigating flexible guidewires and catheters through intricate vascular networks. Modern soft-body physics simulators do not capture the edge cases or interaction dynamics these tools actually exhibit — the bending, buckling and torsion that accumulate under sustained torque and mechanical stress over many episodes.

TESA addresses that gap with scalable real-world data collection across a series of environments, or "gyms", spanning target poses from simple to nearly impossible. The lab is contributing two things to the Open-H Endoluminal ecosystem: a standardized endoluminal dataset (TESA-Data) and a low-cost open-source hardware platform (TESA-Bot). The model is the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery tasks, whose cheap standardized hardware reshaped the science of surgical skill assessment — we want the same for endovascular skills.

The platform is a 2-DOF guidewire and catheter driver with a bill of materials under $100, built around a custom PCB that accepts relative step commands of insertion and rotation, with synchronized motor encoders and an overhead camera acting as a simulated single-plane fluoroscopy view. Roughly ten 3D-printed vascular phantoms — some abstract bifurcations and aneurysms, others 2D projections of anatomy from the NIH 3D library — are backlit so the guidewire can be optically tracked inside the channels.

The target is 30 to 50 hours of synchronized robotic telemetry and vision tracking. Most of it is gathered by a model-free reinforcement learning agent (Soft Actor-Critic) navigating the gyms in real time, with human operators stepping in at bifurcations the agent cannot reach. Automated computer-vision checks detect motor slippage, re-establish the origin, and discard frames showing loops or buckling. Because every experiment uses benchtop phantoms derived from open anatomical models, the dataset carries no HIPAA or PHI constraints.

Everything generated under the project — algorithms, firmware, network weights, CAD, schematics, raw video and spatial metadata — is committed for public release under the OpenMDW-1.1 (Open Medical Data & Hardware) license.
researchers: Neev Zeroni, Tarun Sehgal, Sam Fisher, Gabriel Garso, Amit Manicka, Timothy M. Kowalewski
